h1: Surrogate advertising rules for spirits in India
title: Surrogate Advertising Rules for Spirits | Craft Beer School
desc: What surrogate advertising is, how Indian rules on alcohol advertising and brand extensions work at process level and what teams should check.
teaser: Soda, music and glassware ads that look a lot like whisky ads have a name. Here is how the rules treat them.
standfirst: Direct alcohol advertising is restricted in India, so brands have often promoted other products under the same name. This guide explains surrogate advertising, how the rules on it work at process level and what marketing teams should check before a campaign.
sections: Why the question comes up at all

India restricts direct advertising of alcoholic drinks. The rules governing television programming prohibit advertisements that promote liquor directly or indirectly. Similar restrictions apply across other media. Alcohol is also largely a state subject, so states add their own rules on promotion and display.

Yet alcohol brands are well known. Part of the reason is the brand extension: a soda, packaged water, music, glassware or other product sold under the same brand name as a whisky. Advertising the extension keeps the name in front of people. When the extension exists mainly to advertise the alcohol, that is called surrogate advertising.

The line between a genuine brand extension and a surrogate is about substance. A genuine extension is a real product with real sales and distribution, advertised in its own right. A surrogate is an extension that exists mainly on screen, with little presence in shops, used to promote the alcohol behind it.

The Advertising Standards Council of India (ASCI) has a code chapter and guidelines on alcohol advertising and brand extensions. Consumer protection guidelines on misleading advertisements, issued in 2022, also prohibit surrogate advertising. Both look at whether the extension is genuinely sold and whether the advertisement uses imagery, colours or cues that point to the alcohol product.

Without quoting any specific clause, these are the questions a compliance review usually asks of a brand extension campaign:

  • Is the extension product actually on sale, with real distribution and sales records?
  • Is its advertising proportionate to its business, rather than to the alcohol brand's?
  • Does the advertisement show only the extension product, or does it borrow bottle shapes, glasses, colours, settings or language associated with the whisky?
  • Would a reasonable viewer read it as an advertisement for alcohol?
  • Does it appeal to anyone below the legal drinking age, which each state sets between 18 and 25?

Thresholds and wording change. The current ASCI code, the consumer protection guidelines and the broadcasting rules must be checked for each campaign, with legal advice. This guide is not legal advice.

The same thinking applies beyond television. Sponsoring a music festival, a sports league or a film under a brand name linked to alcohol raises the same questions about whether the alcohol product is being promoted indirectly. Digital channels are covered too. A brand extension post on social media is judged by the same tests as a television spot. Our guide to whisky digital marketing within the rules covers the online side.
What it means for production and supply teams

Surrogate rules sound like a marketing problem, but they reach the plant and the supply chain. If a brand extension must be a genuine product, someone has to make it, pack it, distribute it and record its sales. A soda or water extension needs its own specification, quality checks, pack and route to market. Those records are the evidence that the product is real.

That is also where many organisations are weakest. A brand team may have a strong campaign and a thin trail of production and sales data for the extension behind it.

A sensible minimum is a file per extension holding its product specification, the plant or co-packer that makes it, monthly volumes produced, invoices to distributors and the states where it is sold. Kept up to date every month, that file answers most questions a reviewer could ask. Assembled in a hurry after a complaint, it rarely convinces anyone.
Responsible marketing goes further than the minimum

Many spirits companies follow their own responsible marketing codes that are stricter than the law: no appeal to minors, no link between drinking and driving, no suggestion that alcohol brings social, sexual or sporting success and no health claims. A campaign that passes these codes is far less likely to run into trouble under any of the formal rules.

Our guide to state labelling rules for spirits covers the rules that apply on the bottle itself.

List every brand extension that carries one of your whisky brand names. Against each, note whether it has current sales and distribution records your team could produce tomorrow. Any extension without them is the first item for a conversation with your legal team.
faqs: It is advertising a product that shares a name with an alcohol brand, such as a soda or music, mainly to promote the alcohol indirectly.
Is surrogate advertising allowed in India?
Consumer protection guidelines issued in 2022 prohibit surrogate advertising. ASCI also has guidelines on brand extensions. Rules change, so take legal advice for each campaign.
What makes a brand extension genuine?
A real product with real sales and distribution, advertised in proportion to its own business and without cues pointing to the alcohol brand.
